# Group: Suhas, Mert, Carson, Max

# Our Data

## Primary Dataset: Austin Crime Reports 2003-Present

### Source: https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/crime-reports-bf2b7

This dataset is sourced directly from the Austin Police Department (APD) and is updated weekly. It is a record of every crime report filed by APD officers, with the data being entered online by the officers and subsequently stored in this database.

## Secondary Dataset: Key Economic Indicators in Austin 2007-2025

### Source: https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/key-economic-indicators

This data set is a compilation that pulls from various external sources and integrates them into a single data frame. Specifically, the presence of data for the United States and regions other than Texas confirms that it was compiled from a variety of sources to provide a broader economic context. The inclusion of data beyond Texas simply means there are extra fields in the table that we don't need for a Texas-only analysis.

```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}

# Load in data
crimes <- read.csv("austin.csv")
econ <- read.csv("austin_econ.csv")

```

# Key Objective

Our goal is to evaluate the properties of Austin crime and their relationships with the Texas economy. Our main focus will be on key crime characteristics, including the time of day and year, types and categories of offenses, and geographic location. We will look for patterns and relationships among these characteristics to gain a deeper, more informed understanding of crime within Austin.

A significant part of our work will involve grouping key variables to simplify data visualization and ensure our evaluation captures general patterns. Instead of analyzing time by the minute, for example, we'll focus on specific times of day, and we'll likewise group various crime types into broader categories. These strategic groupings will allow us to draw meaningful connections between different crime cohorts, providing the city of Austin with actionable insights into the crime patterns within its jurisdiction.

## Key Variables

-   **Highest Offense Description**: Tells us what the crime is. Important for us to be able to judge severity and type of crime.
-   **Location Type**: Tells us what type of place the crime occurred. Important to make distinctions between places like homes, stores, etc.
-   **District**: Gives general area of the crime in Austin. Allows us to understand where crimes are occurring in the city.
-   **Occurred Time**: Tells us when the crime occurred so we can determine if crime is more common during certain times of day.
-   **Report Time**: Tells us when the crime was reported and can be combined with occurred time to understand how it takes certain areas to report crimes.
-   **Unemployment in Texas**: Informs on the state of the economy in Texas, allowing us to search for patterns in how crime changes when the economy does.
-   **Retail Gas Price**: Another economic indicator allowing us to understand how crime changes when the economy does.

## Pre-Processing

-   Grouping times, so instead of looking at specific times we can analyze times of day. This is for the main dataset.
-   Converting datetime character vectors to datetime object to make datetime data columns more usable. This is for the main dataset.
-   Create a new column, Net.Response.Date.Time, which measures the time between the date and time between when the crime occurred and when it was reported. This is for the main dataset.
-   Created a new column, timeOfDay, which uses the "Occured Time" column and sorts the crimes into 8 buckets, and assigns the correct label. 12am-3am is Midnight, 3am-6am is Dawn, 6am-9am is Sunrise, 9am-12pm is Morning, 12pm-3pm is Noon, 3pm-6pm is Afternoon, 6pm-9pm is Dusk, and 9pm-12pm is Evening. This is for the main dataset.
-   Created a new column, date, which turns the values stored in the "Month" and "Year" columns from characters into the Date format. This is for the secondary dataset.
-   Created a new column, Year, which takes Occurred.Date.Time and extracts the year from it as a date variable. This is for the main dataset.

```{r, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
#Pre Processing
crimes$Occurred.Date.Time <- as.POSIXct(crimes$Occurred.Date.Time, format = "%m/%d/%Y %H:%M")
crimes$Report.Date.Time <- as.POSIXct(crimes$Report.Date.Time, format = "%m/%d/%Y %H:%M")
crimes$NetResponse.Date.Time <- crimes$Report.Date.Time - crimes$Occurred.Date.Time
crimes$OccurMonth <- format(crimes$Occurred.Date.Time, "%Y-%m")
crimes$ReportMonth <- format(crimes$Report.Date.Time, "%Y-%m")
```

# Linear Regression Model -- Predicting Gas Prices

To better understand the Texas economy we will create a simple model that uses linear regression to show the relationship between produced gas, gas prices, and diesel prices. It's important for us to be well informed on the Texas economy to understand any patterns that may exist between economic changes and frequency of crime.

```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# Linear Regression: predicting gas price given diesel price
retail_gas <- econ$Retail.Gasoline.Price.TX
retail_diesel <- econ$Retail.Diesel.Price.TX
# Extracted gas value in billions
gas_prod <- econ$Gross.Value.Natural.Gas.Production / 1000
gas_diesel_model <- lm(retail_gas ~ retail_diesel + gas_prod)
model_sum <- summary(gas_diesel_model)
model_sum$coefficients

```

## Linear Regression Model Interpretation

The model was constructed using linear regression with two independent/predictor variables and one dependent variable. For every `$`1 increase in diesel price, gas prices increase by `$`0.7878. For every one billion dollar increase in diesel price, gas prices decrease by a minimal `$`0.029. The purpose of this model is to understand how diesel prices and the value of the extracted natural gas in a given month are related to gas prices. From our model, it's clear diesel prices changing has a much stronger correlation that the change of value in natural gas extracted (in billions).

# Visualizations

## Bar Graph -- Average Response Time by Council District

Responding quickly to a crime can be the difference between catching the perpetrator and having to search for days. We want to find out whether or not there are certain districts that have significantly faster or slower response times.

```{r, , message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}

# get numeric value in seconds
crimes$Response.Duration.Seconds <- as.numeric(
  gsub(" secs", "", crimes$NetResponse.Date.Time)
)

# Convert to minutes
crimes$Response.Duration.Minutes <- crimes$Response.Duration.Seconds / 60

# Get average for each district
crimes_summary <- aggregate(
  x = crimes$Response.Duration.Minutes, 
  by = list(District = crimes$Council.District),
  FUN = mean,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

# Name average time column
names(crimes_summary)[2] <- "Average.Response.Time"

# Create plot
ggplot(data = crimes_summary, aes(x = factor(District), y = Average.Response.Time)) +
  geom_col(fill = "skyblue") +
  
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(Average.Response.Time, 1)), 
    vjust = -0.5, 
    size = 3.5
  ) +
    labs(
    title = "Average Incident Response Time by Council District",
    x = "Council District",
    y = "Average Response Time (Minutes)"
  ) +  scale_x_discrete(breaks = as.character(1:10)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 15)),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )

```

## Bar Graph Interpretation

There are some significant disparities in average response time across the districts. District 9 stands out, reporting crimes significantly faster than any other. On the other hand, Districts 7 and 10 consistently exhibit the longest response times. External research strongly correlates faster response times with a much higher crime resolution rate. This key finding suggests that District 9 is exceptionally well-positioned to effectively solve and address crimes.

## Boxplot -- Average Time to Report Crime in Austin (2003-2025)

Not all crimes get solved, but the ones that do start with the crime being reported. This takes someone witnessing the crime or finding something related to the crime scene like the victim or perpetrator. Whether people witnessed the crime or not, reporting can be anywhere from immediate to months and this boxplot will visualize, in general, how long it takes for crimes to get reported.

```{r, , message=FALSE, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE}

#Plot
bp <- boxplot(crimes$NetResponse.Date.Time[crimes$NetResponse.Date.Time > 0], outline = FALSE,
        yaxt = "n", 
        ylab = "Report Time (HRS:MIN:SEC)", 
        main = "Average Time to Report Crime in Austin, TX (2003-2025)",
        sub = "Zero Duration Excluded | Outliers Removed From Plot"
        )

axis(2, at = axTicks(2), labels = as.hms(axTicks(2)))

# Add labels for median, Q1, and Q3
stats <- bp$stats
rownames(stats) <- c("Lower Whisker", "Q1 (25%)", "Median", "Q3 (75%)", "Upper Whisker")

text(x = 0.7, y = stats[2,1], labels = paste("Q1:", as.hms(stats[2,1], 1)), pos = 3, col = "red")
text(x = 0.7, y = stats[3,1], labels = paste("Median:", as.hms(stats[3,1], 1)), pos = 3, col = "blue")
text(x = 0.7, y = stats[4,1], labels = paste("Q3:", as.hms(stats[4,1], 1)), pos = 3, col = "darkgreen")
#line and % at 48 hours
percentile_48 <- round(ecdf(crimes$NetResponse.Date.Time[crimes$NetResponse.Date.Time > 0])(60*60*48)*100, 1)
abline(h = 48 * 60 * 60, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
text(x = 1.25, y = 48 * 60 * 60, labels = paste0("48 Hours: ", percentile_48, "th Percentile"), 
     pos = 3, col = "red", offset = 1)

```

## Boxplot Interpretation

The vast majority (74%) of crimes are reported within 48 hours of reportedly being committed. The median time to report a crime is about 11 and a half hours. Additionally, the time needed to report a crime is heavily right-skewed, indicating significant room for study on what crimes are not reported quickly, and why. This investigation could focus on a variety of aspects such as analyzing what crime types take the longest to report.

## Heatmap -- Crime by Month and District

Just because our data looks at a relatively small area doesn't mean that crime doesn't vary in different parts of the city. By using the district breakdown of Austin we can investigate the amount of crime occurring in each district while also potentially finding times of the year that are more prone to prevalent crime.

```{r, , message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
#Pulling Months and labelling as text
heatmap_crimes <- crimes[,c("Occurred.Date", "APD.District")]
heatmap_crimes$month <- substr(as.character(heatmap_crimes$Occurred.Date), 0, 2)
heatmap_crimes$month <- factor(heatmap_crimes$month, labels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"), levels = c("01", "02", "03", "04", "05", "06", "07", "08", "09", "10", "11", "12"))
heatmap_crimes$month <- factor(heatmap_crimes$month, levels = rev(levels(heatmap_crimes$month)))
heatmap_crimes <- heatmap_crimes[heatmap_crimes$APD.District != "",]

#Turn data into table object
count_table <- table(heatmap_crimes$month, heatmap_crimes$APD.District)
count_table <- count_table[rowSums(count_table) >= 1500, 
               colSums(count_table) >= 1500]

par(mar = c(7, 6, 8, 6))  # Increased margins: c(bottom, left, top, right)
#Plot the table as a heatmap
heatmap(as.matrix(count_table), 
        Colv = NA, 
        Rowv = NA,
        col = colorRampPalette(c("pink", "red"))(50),
        ylab = "Month",
        xlab = "Austin, TX | District | Min. 1500 Reported Crimes | 2003-2025",
        main = "Crime by Month and District",
        cex.main = 0.6)
```

## Heat Map Interpretation

In general, the displayed districts are the only districts in Austin with any significant crime. All districts not displayed have at most an average of 5.68 crimes per month reported. While this seems moderately high, the dataset includes crimes like petty theft, false alarms, and civil disturbance which are ultimately not that serious compared to widespread crime. Thus, it is reasonable to say that the highest concentration of crime in Austin is in districts 1-8, 88, D, and S. We can use this information to further explore the interactions crime has with the general economy in these areas.

## Pie Chart -- Amount of crime by time of day

It's easy to think that most crimes would be committed at night when less people will see. This pie chart allows us to visualize this and see if that assumption really is true. We want to use this pie chart to inform the APD on when the most crimes are occurring as it could help them schedule the amount of on-duty cops more effectively.

```{r, , message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
pieBuckets <- c("Midnight","Dawn","Sunrise","Morning","Noon","Afternoon","Dusk","Evening")
crimes$timeOfDay <- cut(crimes$`Occurred.Time`, breaks = c(1, 300, 600, 900, 1200, 1500, 1800, 2100, 2400), 
                         labels = pieBuckets)

pie(table(crimes$timeOfDay), label = pieBuckets, 
    col = c("darkblue", "darkgoldenrod2", "gold1", "forestgreen","indianred3","khaki2","palegreen1","steelblue2"),
    main = "Amount of Crimes by Time of Day")
```

## Pie Chart Interpretation

The distribution of crimes is generally evenly spread across the day, only decreasing significantly during the times of dawn and sunrise (3-9AM). The three periods of time with the greatest amount of crime are afternoon, dusk, and evening. This was quite surprising, as we expected the data to show that most crimes occured after sundown, however the split of crime between when it was light (dawn to afternoon) and dark (dusk to midnight) is nearly 50/50, with the light portion of the day having a majority of the crimes.

## Mosaic Plot -- Frequent Crimes by Time of Day

This plot will build on the pie chart and breakdown when crimes are occurring by the most frequent crime types. The pie chart is a good start and gives us general information, but in this mosaic plot we can see when the most common crime types are occurring.

```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}

# Two-way table of crime type vs. time of day bucket
tab <- table(crimes$Highest.Offense.Description, crimes$timeOfDay)
# Keep only the top 10 offenses 
phrase_freq <- sort(table(crimes$Highest.Offense.Description), decreasing = TRUE)
top_offenses <- names(head(phrase_freq, 10))
tab_top <- tab[top_offenses, ]
# Wrap labels
wrapped_names <- sapply(rownames(tab_top), function(x) {
  x_clean <- gsub("-", " - ", x)  
  paste(strwrap(x_clean, width = 12), collapse = "\n")
})
rownames(tab_top) <- wrapped_names
rownames(tab_top)[rownames(tab_top) == "ASSAULT\nW/INJURY -\nFAM/DATE\nVIOL"] <- "ASSAULT"
# Make Plot
par(mar = c(6, 6, 6, 6))

mosaicplot(tab_top,
           main = "Most Frequent Crime Types by Time of Day (Austin, TX)",
           xlab = "",
           ylab = "",
           col = c("darkblue", "darkgoldenrod2", "gold1", "forestgreen","indianred3","khaki2","palegreen1","steelblue2"),
           las = 2,
           cex.axis = 0.7)

```

## Mosaic Interpretation

Most of the frequent crime types occur during the daytime, which is consistent with the pie chart. Intuitively, DWI crimes typically occur during nighttime since people are more likely to drink at night. Interestingly, vehicular crimes like burgalry or auto theft typically occur in the later parts of the day, but not very often at nighttime. This is consistent with other crimes like criminal mischief, assault, and other disturbances, but not to the same extent. This finding could serve as a jumping point into further questions about why that may be the case.

## Line Chart -- Unemployment & Gas Prices against time since 2007 by month.

These are our main economic indicators so it's critical we visualize how they are related, if they are related at all. By understanding this relationship we can better utilize each piece of information when we look to connect them to information on crimes.

```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
#Pre processing
econ$date <- as.Date(paste(econ$Year, econ$Month, "01", sep = "-"))
x_value_time <- econ$date[25:247]

y_values_gasPrice <- econ$Retail.Gasoline.Price.TX[25:247]
y_values_unemployment <- econ$Unemployment.TX[25:247]

#Plot
y_min <- min(c(y_values_gasPrice, y_values_unemployment), na.rm = TRUE)
y_max <- max(c(y_values_gasPrice, y_values_unemployment), na.rm = TRUE)

y_margin <- (y_max - y_min) * 0.05
ylim_range <- c(y_min - y_margin, y_max + y_margin)

plot(x_value_time, y_values_gasPrice, type = "n",  # "n" means no points, just a blank canvas
     xlab = "Time", ylab = "Values",
     main = "Retail Gasoline Price vs Unemployment Rate",
     ylim = ylim_range)  

lines(smooth.spline(x_value_time, y_values_gasPrice), col = "darkblue", lwd = 2)

lines(smooth.spline(x_value_time, y_values_unemployment), col = "darkred", lwd = 2)

legend("topleft", legend = c("Gasoline Price ($)", "Unemployment Rate (%)"),
       col = c("darkblue", "darkred"), lwd = 2)
```

## Line Chart Interpretation

This was secondary data that we wanted to analyze to help us understand the trends in crimes in Austin. Gas prices (in Tx) and unemployment (in Tx) are often used as key economic indicators, therefore we plotted them against time to gain insight into the conditions that might contribute to a rise or decline in crime. This extra dimension of our analysis will allow us to understand unique period of time (such as the COVID Lockdowns and the associated impacts on crime).


## Lollipop Chart -- Family Violence Reports over Time

To better understand the prevalence of family violence in crimes, we wanted to study how the proportion of crimes reported as family violence changed over time. This study may also inform us on reporting practices, and whether people became more willing to report family violence over time. 

```{r,  message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
crime_table <- table(crimes$Family.Violence, crimes$ReportMonth)
crime_table <- crime_table[rowSums(crime_table) > 100,]
crime_df <- as.data.frame(t(crime_table))
crime_df$ReportMonth <- rownames(crime_df)
crime_df <- as.data.frame(crime_table)
colnames(crime_df) <- c("Family.Violence", "ReportMonth", "Freq")
crime_wide <- reshape(crime_df, 
                     idvar = "ReportMonth",
                     timevar = "Family.Violence",
                     direction = "wide")
colnames(crime_wide) <- c("ReportMonth", "No", "Yes")
colnames(crime_wide) <- gsub("Freq\\.", "", colnames(crime_wide))
crime_table <- crime_wide[, c("ReportMonth", "Yes", "No")]
crime_table$Total <- crime_table$Yes + crime_table$No
crime_table$Pct_Yes <- (crime_table$Yes / crime_table$Total) * 100
crime_table$Pct_No <- (crime_table$No / crime_table$Total) * 100
crime_pct <- crime_table[, c("ReportMonth", "Pct_Yes", "Pct_No")]

selected_months <- crime_pct$ReportMonth[seq(1, nrow(crime_pct), by = 24)]

ggplot(crime_pct, aes(x=ReportMonth, y=Pct_Yes)) +
  geom_segment( aes(x=ReportMonth, xend=ReportMonth, y=0, yend=Pct_Yes), color = "skyblue") +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Family Violence Cases Reported Over Time",
    x = "",
    y = "Cases Reported as Family Violence (%)",
    subtitle = "Austin, TX (2003-2025)"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(breaks = selected_months) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Lollipop Chart Interpretation
From 2003 through 2025, the proportion of reported crimes that were family violence cases increased by over 50%. Logically, this increase can be attributed to increase in family violence cases, an increase in reporting of these cases, and the general decrease of crime which increases the proportion of stable family violence cases. While it is possible that one of these cases makes up the majority of the increase, such a drastic change in reports is likely due to some combination of the three.  

## Area Chart -- Occurrence of Crime at Key Locations



```{r,  message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
#Make a new column based off the Occured.Date.Time column (already formatted when
#we made our boxplot), which is only the year
crimes$year <- format(as.POSIXct(crimes$Occurred.Date.Time), "%Y")

# These are the relevant locations we will be examining
relevant_location_types <- c(
  "GROCERY / SUPERMARKET",
  "CONVENIENCE STORE",
  "RESIDENCE / HOME",
  "HWY / ROAD / ALLEY/ STREET/ SIDEWALK",
  "PARKING /DROP LOT/ GARAGE",
  "HOTEL / MOTEL / ETC.",
  "DRUG STORE / DOCTOR'S OFFICE / HOSPITAL",
  "COMMERCIAL / OFFICE BUILDING",
  "BAR / NIGHTCLUB",
  "RESTAURANT"
)

#Gets the total crimes per year from the full dataset
total_crimes_per_year <- table(crimes$year)

# Filtering the crimes to include only the ones that are relevant
crimes_filtered <- subset(crimes, Location.Type %in% relevant_location_types)

#Create a table containing the year and how many of each different type of crime
#happened that year.
crime_counts_table <- table(crimes_filtered$year, crimes_filtered$Location.Type)

# Convert to data frame
crime_counts_df <- as.data.frame(crime_counts_table)
colnames(crime_counts_df) <- c("year", "Location.Type", "count")

#Calculates percentages based on total crimes 
#(not just based on the crime locations we're focusing on)
years <- unique(crime_counts_df$year)
crime_counts_df$percentage <- 0

for(yr in years) {
  year_mask <- crime_counts_df$year == yr
  #Uses total crimes from all data to calculate percentage
  year_total <- total_crimes_per_year[yr]
  crime_counts_df$percentage[year_mask] <- (crime_counts_df$count[year_mask] / as.numeric(year_total)) * 100
}

# Ensure that the years will be treated as numbers instead of date variables.
crime_counts_df$year <- as.numeric(as.character(crime_counts_df$year))

# Plot with percentages
ggplot(crime_counts_df, aes(x = year, y = percentage, fill = Location.Type)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 1) +  
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Selected Crime Locations as Percentage of All Crimes",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Percentage of Total Crimes (%)",
       fill = "Location Type") +
  # Shows every other year in the x-label for a cleaner look.
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(min(crime_counts_df$year), 
                                  max(crime_counts_df$year), 
                                  by = 2)) +
  # Format y-axis as percentage
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A", "#984EA3",
                               "#FF7F00", "#FFFF33", "#A65628", "#F781BF",
                               "#999999", "#66C2A5")) +
  # Fix the x-axis label
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

## Slope Chart -- Total Thefts by Type & Year

Of all the crimes, theft occurs quite frequently, leading to a variety of types of theft occurring. In this graph we look to better understand the most common types of theft, how often they occur, and if there are any patterns over time.

```{r,  message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# Get all theft rows
theft_rows <- grepl("THEFT", crimes$Highest.Offense.Description, ignore.case = TRUE)


# Create df with thefts, year
theft_crimes_df <- crimes[theft_rows, c("Highest.Offense.Description", "year")]
theft_crimes_df$Highest.Offense.Description[
  theft_crimes_df$Highest.Offense.Description == "THEFT"
] <- "GENERAL THEFT"

# Get Amount of thefts in each year
theft_summary <- aggregate(
    x = theft_crimes_df$Highest.Offense.Description,
    by = list(year = theft_crimes_df$year, theft_type = theft_crimes_df$Highest.Offense.Description),
    FUN = length
)
colnames(theft_summary) <- c("year", "theft_type", "total_thefts")

# Find Most Common Types of Theft
all_time_counts <- tapply(
    X = theft_summary$total_thefts,
    INDEX = theft_summary$theft_type,
    FUN = sum
)
top_7_theft_types <- names(sort(all_time_counts, decreasing = TRUE))[1:7]

# Only keep top 7 most common types of theft
filtered_theft_summary <- theft_summary[theft_summary$theft_type %in% top_7_theft_types, ]


# Get average consumer confidence by year
avg_confidence_by_year <- aggregate(
    x = econ$Consumer.Confidence.Index.TX,
    by = list(year = econ$Year),
    FUN = mean,
    na.rm = TRUE
)
avg_confidence_by_year <- na.omit(avg_confidence_by_year)
colnames(avg_confidence_by_year)[colnames(avg_confidence_by_year) == "x"] <- "Consumer.Index"


# Join confidence and crimes
theft_type_consumer_confidence <- merge(
    x = theft_summary,
    y = avg_confidence_by_year,
    by = "year",
    all = FALSE
)

# Create slope chart
filtered_theft_summary$year <- as.factor(filtered_theft_summary$year)
theft_type_label_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(filtered_theft_summary, filtered_theft_summary$theft_type), 
                                               function(x) x[which.max(as.numeric(as.character(x$year))), ]))

ggplot(filtered_theft_summary, aes(x = year, y = total_thefts, group = theft_type, color = theft_type)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") + 
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right", 
    plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10) 
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Thefts by Type (2003 - 2023)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Total Thefts",
    color = "Theft Type"
  )

```

## Slope Chart Interpretation

The drop in General Theft (unspecified) could be because reports are more detailed now, total thefts have declined, or both simultaneously. A key trend shows shoplifting has steadily dropped since 2013, while auto theft surged from 2017 to 2023 but has since fallen even faster. It's notable that two of the most common types of theft are specific crimes: bicycle theft and license plate theft. This indicates that many theft issues stem from people stealing lower-value items that are nonetheless essential for daily life.
